rationale: The student added both numerators and denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). A number line divided into fifths demonstrates that adding fifths means taking hops along fifth-sized intervals, keeping the denominator constant at 5. To ensure a different answer from the student's problem (which resulted in 3/5), we use 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5.

script.focus: the tick marks and denominator remain fifths as you hop forward

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: the tick marks and denominator remain fifths as you hop forward

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The demonstration explicitly addresses adding numerators while keeping the denominator constant by showing hops along a fifths number line. Moving from fraction bars to a number line provides an effective alternate representation, clearly reinforcing that the size of each step remains 1/5.
judgement.verdict: A teacher would definitely use this detour right now because the number-line hops make it visual and intuitive that the unit size (fifths) does not change when adding.
